texto:
On October 28, 2026, Vibe, the self-serve streaming TV advertising platform Walmart bought in August, began letting all of its advertisers target campaigns with audience segments that Walmart builds from its own shopping data. A companion article from Walmart Connect, Walmart's advertising business, followed on October 29 and described the launch as the first major integration milestone since the acquisition. The segments arrive with an AI agent, called Smart select, that proposes a starting list for each campaign - and with a measurement arrangement that, on the evidence of both announcements, still runs through Vibe's own tools rather than Walmart's sales records.
In Short
Walmart knows what millions of people buy in its stores and on its website, and it has started letting advertisers on Vibe, a TV ad platform it owns, show streaming TV ads to households grouped by that shopping. A skincare brand, for example, can pick "skin care" shoppers, and a small AI helper can suggest which groups to pick. The catch is that the results are still checked on the advertiser's own website, not against what people later buy at Walmart.
What arrived on October 28
According to Vibe's product update, titled "Introducing Walmart Audiences on Vibe," the segments are "available to all Vibe users starting today," a line dated October 28, 2026. The post was last updated on October 29. Advertisers find the segments in an existing part of the campaign builder called In-Market & Interests, where Walmart-supplied segments carry a "by Walmart" label. No new campaign type is required, and campaigns already running are untouched. According to Vibe, existing campaigns "keep running exactly as configured."
Walmart Connect's article, published on October 29 under the headline "Walmart's first-party audiences are now available in Vibe," frames the move in broader terms. "In the first major integration milestone since Walmart acquired Vibe in August, Vibe advertisers can now use available Walmart Audiences to build CTV campaigns directly in Vibe's campaign builder," the article states. The word "available" matters: neither company says whether every segment Walmart Connect sells elsewhere is offered on Vibe, or only part of the catalog.
The division of labour is spelled out. According to Walmart Connect, it "builds and maintains Walmart Audiences, while Vibe continues to manage campaign buying, optimization, measurement and reporting." Walmart supplies the data. Vibe runs everything else.
Arthur Querou, co-founder and chief executive of Vibe, is the only named spokesperson in either announcement. "We built Vibe so performance marketers could hold streaming TV to the same standard as search and social: targeted, measurable and easy to test," Querou said in the Walmart Connect article. "Walmart Audiences add a more precise layer of targeting rooted in what households actually buy. Combined with measurement in the tools marketers already trust and the flexibility to test, advertisers have a clear path to make CTV part of their media plan."
Two kinds of segment
According to Vibe, the catalog contains two types of audience, and both can be combined in one campaign.
Personas
Personas group Walmart customers "based on life stage, lifestyle, interests, and shopping habits, including at seasonal moments." Vibe's examples are women's beauty, men's grooming, healthy living, home gourmet cooks, recent movers, new parents and upper-tier spenders. That last one stands out: Walmart is offering a segment defined by how much its customers spend, not only by what they put in the basket.
Seasonal personas, according to the post, "are derived from customer shopping habits tied to holidays and events on the retail calendar," with examples running from Valentine's Day and Mother's Day to "Big 6 Shopping Days" and Winter holidays. Vibe does not say which six days make up the Big 6. Two more seasonal personas surface in the post's examples: a "New Year, New You" persona for January and a Tax Day persona for March.
Category buyers
Category buyers are Walmart customers grouped "based on what they buy or are showing intent to buy," organised by department. Vibe lists pet supplies, baby, food and beverages, electronics, automotive and crafts, "and more." The granularity runs from "segments as broad as dog supplies" to "as specific as reptile food, quilting, whole bean coffee, or diesel exhaust fluid."
Walmart Connect's article draws the line between past and expected purchases. Advertisers "can choose to reach recent category buyers, customers showing signals that they may purchase soon, or both." An illustration published with the Vibe post shows how that appears on screen: category segments such as Skin care and Home Decor carry an audience type labelled "Recent + In-market," while Healthy living and New home buyers are labelled "Persona." The in-market half of that pairing is a prediction about future buying; the "recent" half is a record of past purchases.
Each segment shows its estimated household count across Vibe before it is added, according to the post, and the estimated reach for the whole selection updates in real time as segments are added or removed. The counts are estimates, and they are counted in households, the unit in which streaming TV is sold.
How many segments?
Neither announcement says. Adweek, reporting on October 29, put the figure at more than 3,300 segments built on Walmart's web and in-store shopping data. ContentGrip, on October 30, cited a claim of more than 3,000 segments on Vibe's public homepage. The Vibe post itself only concedes that "a catalog this size takes a lot of scrolling."
Smart select: the agent that picks first
The scrolling problem is the stated reason for Smart select. When an advertiser opens In-Market & Interests, the builder offers two routes: Smart select or Select manually.
Four inputs
According to Vibe, Smart select reads four inputs: the advertiser's website, the advertiser category "and any category rules," the creatives uploaded to the campaign, and the budget and schedule. Advertisers can add free-text context, such as a product line to push or a customer type to avoid. Vibe does not define what category rules are or who sets them.
The mechanism is described plainly. According to the post, the agent matches the advertiser's inputs against "the names of the available Walmart Audiences," ranks segments by relevance, and checks the combined household count against the budget and flight dates. That detail is significant. The ranking compares an advertiser's inputs with segment names; nothing in the description says the agent looks at which segments have produced sales for similar advertisers, or at the overlap between an advertiser's customers and Walmart's.
The worked example
Vibe walks through one case: a direct-to-consumer skincare brand selling on its own site, with a $25,000 budget running from October 1 to November 30. Smart select, according to the post, might keep four category segments - skin care, face serums, facial moisturizers and skin care sets - plus the women's beauty and Big 6 Shopping Days personas, all "scoring 84% relevance or higher" and "covering 33.2M households across Vibe's platform," with five more suggestions listed below for wider reach.
The household figure is a pool, not a forecast of delivery. A rough calculation by PPC Land shows the gap. Premium CTV prices had climbed to $43 per thousand impressions ahead of the November midterms, according to Nola Ladd of Collective Measures, speaking to Digiday. At that price, $25,000 buys roughly 581,000 impressions - enough for about 1.75% of 33.2 million households to see the ad once. Vibe's own prices are not disclosed in either announcement and may well be lower, but the order of magnitude explains why the agent checks the household count against the budget: the question is whether the pool is large enough to spend into, not whether the campaign will reach all of it. Spread over the 61-day flight, the example budget comes to about $410 a day.
One sentence in the example sits awkwardly with the next. The post says the agent "even reads what will resonate the most" with an advertiser's creative. Yet in the same example, according to Vibe, "no creative had been uploaded yet, so the agent worked from the website, category rules, and budget, and flagged that it skipped creatives." The disclosure is useful - "If an input is missing, the agent says so" - but the published example does not show the creative-reading step at work.
What a relevance score is not
On one point Vibe is careful. "Relevance is an estimate of how closely a segment aligns with the inputs the agent considered. It is not a prediction of campaign performance," the post states. The illustration shows scores ranging from 97% for a Fashion trendsetter persona down to 79% for a suggested Wellness buyers segment of 1.8 million households. A segment scoring 97% could sell nothing at all. The number measures fit with the inputs, not sales.
Nothing launches by itself
"Nothing goes live from Smart select on its own," according to Vibe. Its picks land in the campaign's audience list, where advertisers can remove any segment, switch a segment's audience type or add segments from a "not targeted, suggested next" row, each shown with a relevance score and household count. In the illustration, that row offers Apparel shoppers at 5.9 million households, Wellness buyers at 1.8 million, Electronics shoppers at 1.2 million and Beauty buyers at 993,000.
Walmart Connect has been building agents into its own tools too. It said in January that 97% of queries to its advertising assistant were unique, as it pushed AI features into the Walmart Connect Ad Center.
Where the segments sit in a campaign
Walmart Audiences sit alongside the targeting already available on Vibe, according to the post, and "don't replace it." Vibe Custom Audiences, which are customer lists advertisers sync to Vibe, and Web Audiences, which are people who visited the advertiser's site, keep their own sections of the builder. Location, schedule and placement controls are unchanged.
Vibe sketches a pairing: Walmart category buyers to find new households in a category, then Web Audiences to retarget those who visited the advertiser's site after seeing the ad.
Inside the Walmart section, the combination logic is an "or," not an "and." According to Vibe, a household that matches at least one of the selected segments is included. Every added segment therefore widens the audience. The post describes no way, within In-Market & Interests, to require that a household match two segments at once - new parents who also buy whole bean coffee, for instance.
For advertisers already running broad interest targeting on Vibe, the post proposes a first test: duplicate the campaign, replace the interest targeting with a few Walmart category buyer segments that match the product, and run both side by side. That compares two targeting approaches. Whether it isolates the effect of Walmart's data depends on how Vibe splits delivery and audiences between the two campaigns, which the post does not cover.
The measurement question
This is where the launch departs most clearly from Walmart Connect's usual pitch.
Walmart Connect's measurement page describes closed-loop measurement, "powered by our first-party data," that "ties ad exposure - across Walmart's digital properties and offsite channels - to sales on Walmart's site and in stores." According to the page, when a customer who saw an ad makes a related purchase at Walmart, Walmart Connect recognises and reports it, with results available in near real time through the self-serve Walmart Connect Ad Center. The page lists attribution, incrementality, brand impact and campaign insights among its evaluation methods. It also cites the scale behind the data: about 150 million customers served online and in stores each week in the US, sourced to Walmart annual report papers of March 14, 2025, and more than 4,600 US stores, sourced to Walmart first-party data from February 2025. The October 29 article links to that page from the phrase "Walmart commerce signals."
The Vibe launch describes something else. According to Walmart Connect's own article, "Advertisers can measure results through Vibe's existing tools, including purchase-level attribution on their own sites and incrementality testing." The Vibe post makes no claim that Vibe campaigns are measured against purchases at Walmart. Walmart's purchase data decides who sees the ad; the advertiser's own website decides whether it worked.
Set that against what was said in June. When the agreement was announced on June 23, Vibe's own announcement described the combination as pairing its self-serve platform with Walmart's commerce audiences, closed-loop measurement and VIZIO, and said advertisers would be able to measure campaigns through Walmart's commerce capabilities. PPC Land's report on the deal noted at the time that Vibe's measurement could, after integration, attribute spend to Walmart purchases. Walmart Connect calls the October launch "an early step." The audiences have arrived. The closed loop, on the evidence of these documents, has not.
For the brands in Vibe's own examples, the absence may matter less than it first appears. A DTC skincare label selling on its own site, a moving company, a fitness app and a tax software brand do not sell through Walmart's tills, so a Walmart sales report would have little to show them. For consumer goods brands stocked at Walmart, it matters more. Walmart has offered that loop through other routes: Spotify said in October that eligible campaigns bought through Walmart DSP could connect exposure to outcomes across Walmart's digital properties and more than 4,600 stores, and Yahoo DSP's integration came with closed-loop Walmart sales measurement on VIZIO inventory when it was announced in May.
Vibe's website, meanwhile, advertises a "2.5x average ROAS" beside a 4.8 out of 5 rating on G2 and "500+ channels available." No method, period or sample accompanies the ROAS figure.
What the announcements leave out
Several details a buyer would expect are missing from both documents:
- Price. Neither says whether Walmart Audiences carry a data fee on top of media costs. Adweek's October 29 report described access as requiring no contract.
- Matching. Walmart's data describes shoppers; Vibe sells TV households. Neither document explains how a Walmart customer becomes a streaming household, or what share of a segment can be matched. In an Adstra study reported in July, only 23% of residential IP addresses reached their intended geographic target, a reminder that household identity on television is imperfect.
- Freshness. How often "recent" buyer segments are refreshed is not stated.
- Minimums. No minimum spend or minimum audience size is mentioned. By comparison, LinkedIn data in CTV carried a $50,000 minimum over 30 days on its DSP routes when Microsoft Monetize launched it in May.
- Geography. The documents do not explicitly limit availability to the US, though every Walmart figure cited is a US figure.
- Results. No campaign results, case studies or test outcomes accompany the launch.
Walmart's streaming build-out
The Vibe integration is the latest step in a sequence that began with television hardware. Walmart agreed to buy VIZIO for about $2.3 billion in February 2024, gaining a smart TV operating system and its ad inventory. By February 2026, Walmart reported nearly $6.4 billion in global advertising revenue for fiscal 2026, up 46%, with VIZIO advertising growing at triple digits in the fourth quarter.
Spring 2026 brought a run of openings. VIZIO appeared as a media type in a beta section of the Walmart Connect Ad Center in April. On April 27, Walmart Connect opened CTV buying to all advertisers through Connect Select, reporting that its CTV campaigns delivered a median of 44% new-to-brand buyers in fiscal 2026. A day later came the Scintilla API, which opened about 500 retail data elements to approved partners. In June, Walmart Connect and Google described a closed proof of concept bringing Walmart purchase data into DV360 for YouTube ads.
Then came Vibe. Walmart announced the agreement on June 23, and PPC Land reported that Vibe served more than 10,000 advertisers, offered access to more than 500 apps and channels, and had raised a $22.5 million Series A in February 2024 and a $50 million Series B in October 2025. Neither side disclosed the price, which Chain Store Age and Talk Business & Politics reported at $1.4 billion. Walmart said on August 4 that the acquisition was complete and that Vibe had joined Walmart Connect. When Walmart reported second-quarter results for fiscal 2027 in August, global advertising had grown 38%, with Walmart Connect in the US up 43% excluding VIZIO. Chief Financial Officer John David Rainey put the cost of acquiring and integrating Vibe at about 20 basis points of headwind to full-year operating income growth.
Vibe has kept a brisk release schedule since the deal closed. Its product updates feed lists Twilio Segment sending conversions to Vibe on October 13; 450 apps launched on Vibe's Developer Platform since June, announced on October 20; and brand lift measurement for select enterprise brands with Upwave, DISQO and Kantar on October 27. After the Walmart launch came a Higgsfield integration on November 2, for generating 15- or 30-second commercials and launching them as streaming campaigns in one conversation, and an Amperity connection on November 5, for turning unified customer profiles into CTV audiences.
Why this matters for marketers
Who gets access is the first point. Walmart's earlier television routes ran through Walmart DSP, through deals on VIZIO and partner inventory, or through other buying platforms. Vibe is a self-serve tool built for smaller and growth-stage advertisers, and the Walmart segments now sit in its campaign builder for every user. Amazon took a similar path in October 2023 with Sponsored TV, which came with no minimum spend for vendors and sellers, and Roku launched Ads Manager in September 2024 for performance marketers used to search and social. Pinterest's agreement to buy tvScientific in December 2025 pointed the same way. The difference with Vibe is that the data source is a retailer's shopping records rather than a streaming service's viewing data. Walmart Connect makes the point itself: the audiences are "built from real customer shopping behavior, not simply what content someone watches."
Who the data is for is the second. Every brand in Vibe's examples - DTC skincare, moving services, a fitness app, tax software - sells somewhere other than Walmart. What does a tax software company gain from a retailer's shopping records? The post's only answer is a Tax Day persona in March. Retail media has traditionally earned its keep with brands stocked on the retailer's shelves. Walmart's purchase records are now offered as a general targeting layer for streaming TV, reaching well beyond the brands it sells. Whether retail data performs better in that role remains an open question. The Trade Desk claimed in October that campaigns using retail data showed 41% higher ROAS than those without, a figure PPC Land reported came without a sample size or attribution model.
The third point is the measurement trade-off. Querou's pitch is that streaming TV can be held "to the same standard as search and social." The measurement offered at launch is attribution on the advertiser's own site and incrementality testing. Closing the loop between a television screen and a purchase remains the medium's hardest problem: members of IAB Europe's CTV working group named cross-device attribution and fragmented identifiers as the main barriers in March. Walmart owns one of the largest sets of purchase records in US retail. On Vibe, for now, those records choose the audience but do not grade the result.

Summary
Who: Vibe, the self-serve streaming TV advertising platform Walmart acquired in August 2026, and Walmart Connect, Walmart's advertising business, which builds and maintains the Walmart Audiences. Arthur Querou, Vibe's co-founder and chief executive, is the named spokesperson. The launch affects Vibe's advertisers, which numbered more than 10,000 at the time of the deal.
What: Walmart Audiences, segments built from Walmart customers' online and in-store shopping, are available in Vibe's campaign builder as personas (such as new parents, recent movers or upper-tier spenders, plus seasonal moments) and category buyers (from dog supplies to diesel exhaust fluid). An AI agent, Smart select, ranks segments by how closely their names match an advertiser's website, category, creatives and budget; nothing goes live without review. Measurement runs through Vibe's existing tools, meaning purchase-level attribution on advertisers' own sites and incrementality testing, not Walmart's closed-loop sales measurement.
When: Vibe announced availability for all users on October 28, 2026, and updated its post on October 29. Walmart Connect published its article on October 29, 2026, 12 weeks after the acquisition closed on August 4.
Where: Inside the In-Market & Interests section of Vibe's campaign builder, for streaming TV campaigns. Every Walmart figure cited in the materials is a US figure.
Why: Walmart Connect calls it the first major integration milestone since the acquisition and "an early step" in combining Vibe's platform with Walmart's customer data. For marketers, it puts a retailer's purchase records into a self-serve TV buying tool for smaller advertisers, including brands that do not sell at Walmart, while leaving open questions on price, household matching and whether Walmart's in-store sales measurement will follow.
